Base-model few-shot prompts use three human-written proofs sampled from the validation set; SFT and RL use CoT or non-CoT guiding prompts. Generation uses temperature 1, top-p 0.95, maximum 2,048 tokens, and Lean 4 verification with a 300-second time limit.

The validation set is used for expert iteration in SFT. Base-model few-shot prompts use three correct proofs generated by DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL from the validation set; SFT and RL use CoT or non-CoT guiding prompts. confounds.name: Random-split results may reflect memorization of similar theorems or proofs
confounds.detail: Human-written Lean files often contain similar theorems, sometimes with identical proofs, so a model may prove test theorems by memorizing training examples rather than generalizing.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on the novel_premises split, which requires test proofs to use at least one premise never used in training, and report results separately from the random split.

confounds.name: Incorrect proof-environment judgments could distort measured performance

confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure misjudgments on ground-truth proofs: LeanDojo reports 1.4%, compared with 21.1% for the existing tool discussed in the paper.

confounds.name: GPT-4 may have seen publicly available ground-truth proofs

confounds.ruled_out_by: No measurement ruling this out is stated; the paper notes the possibility and refers to Appendix C.2 for details.

evidence_standards.name: Theorem-proving evaluation budget
evidence_standards.detail: Pass@1 allows one attempt per theorem, with proof search limited to 10 minutes of wall time; tactics are combined using best-first search. The paper does not report seed-based variance, confidence intervals, statistical tests, or a margin for treating results as ties.

controls.name: Curated context alongside full-repository context

controls.rules_out: A difference between conditions can be attributed to adding broader repository context while keeping the relevant dependencies available in both; the paper describes the gap as measuring this added context.

confounds.name: Contamination from closed-weight models' pretraining data
confounds.detail: Because the benchmark is drawn from public GitHub repositories, a model could succeed through memorization rather than repository-scale reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports that dependency depth is strongly correlated with failure and says this suggests memorization alone is insufficient, while explicitly stating that contamination cannot be fully ruled out.

confounds.name: Full-repository context supplies useful cues outside the ground-truth dependency closure
confounds.detail: Structurally similar proofs or recurring abstraction patterns in unrelated files could compensate for the larger search space and affect the curated-versus-full success gap.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper gives an illustrative analogous proof but explicitly says this is not a causal attribution for the aggregate gap.

confounds.name: Alternative causes of Goedel-Prover-V2's poor transfer
confounds.detail: Project-specific abstractions, long dependency chains, distribution shift from mathematics benchmarks, or the Pass@8 budget could account for its low success without any one being the cause.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not isolated by a measurement; the paper explicitly states that it does not isolate why Goedel-Prover-V2 transfers poorly.

evidence_standards.name: Pass@8 with up to 3 repair rounds for general-purpose LLMs
evidence_standards.detail: Sample 8 candidate proof scripts; for failing scripts, allow up to 3 repair rounds using compiler errors, relevant code lines, and the current proof state. A task counts as solved if any candidate or repair passes Lean verification.

S1–S4 incorrect proofs are filtered for Lean syntax validity, type-check failure, and non-trivial errors; S3 Python-code examples bypass Lean validation. No split is specified.

metrics.name: Pointwise accuracy
metrics.caveat: Pointwise scoring is immune to pairwise position bias but does not measure direct comparison or order consistency; the paper recommends reporting it alongside pairwise accuracy.

metrics.name: Pairwise accuracy (position-consistent)
metrics.caveat: Pairwise judgments show substantial position bias; accuracy requires correct predictions in both orderings, and the paper reports normal and reversed ordering results as well.

metrics.name: Accuracy by error strategy
metrics.caveat: High performance on Python injection can reflect recognizing Python rather than understanding formal proof correctness; the paper reports results separately by strategy.

metrics.name: Normal-order accuracy
metrics.caveat: A correct-first result can be inflated by preference for the first proof; the paper reports reversed-order accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: Reversed-order accuracy
metrics.caveat: A correct-second result can be affected by preference for the second proof; the paper reports normal-order accuracy alongside it.

metrics.name: Consistency
metrics.caveat: Consistency alone can be high when a model consistently selects the wrong proof; the paper reports accuracy and agreement alongside it.

metrics.name: Agreement
metrics.caveat: Agreement across orderings can be high despite incorrect preferences; the paper reports accuracy alongside it.

controls.name: Swapped pairwise presentation order
controls.detail: Each proof pair is evaluated with the correct proof first and with the correct proof second.
controls.rules_out: A preference caused merely by which proof is presented first or second; pairwise accuracy counts a prediction as correct only if both orderings are correct.

confounds.name: Pairwise performance differences may reflect position bias rather than proof evaluation
confounds.detail: A model that favors the first or second proof could appear to distinguish correct from incorrect proofs when their order is favorable.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure normal and reversed ordering separately and require correct predictions in both orderings for position-consistent pairwise accuracy.

confounds.name: Generated examples may contain unintended artifacts or inconsistencies
confounds.detail: Model scores could reflect artifacts in generated pairs rather than the intended proof-correctness distinction.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Automatic Lean validation for S1–S4 and manual inspection of a random sample of 50 pairs; the authors note that manual inspection covers only a subset.

evidence_standards.name: Evaluation decoding and scoring
evidence_standards.detail: Results use nucleus sampling with temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.75. Accuracy is mean correctness over all examples; pairwise correctness requires correct predictions in both orderings. The paper reports no seeds, variance estimates, or statistical significance tests.

metrics.name: Effective accuracy
metrics.caveat: Giving credit to verified proofs of excessively simplified statements can overstate performance in an Olympiad setting; the paper also reports an Olympiad-setting score that gives those proofs no credit.

metrics.name: Autoformalization accuracy (formalization accuracy)
metrics.caveat: LLM evaluation can mark semantically incorrect translations as correct, including discrepancies that materially change meaning; the paper reports expert human verification alongside LLM-based evaluation. Outputs that fail Lean compilation are excluded.

metrics.name: Theorem prover accuracy (whole-proof generation accuracy)
metrics.caveat: Accuracy on the original benchmark can be affected by unprovable statements and by statements simplified relative to the source problems; the paper also reports results on corrected versions and on repaired, simplified, and excessively simplified subsets.

confounds.name: LLM judges may overestimate autoformalization accuracy
confounds.detail: An apparently high translation accuracy may reflect false-positive judgments by an LLM rather than semantically faithful formalizations; the authors report that small discrepancies can change statement meaning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They manually verify translations with Lean experts and report human-verified accuracy alongside LLM-evaluated accuracy.

confounds.name: Apparent theorem-prover failures may originate in mistranslation rather than proving ability
confounds.detail: A prover can fail because the autoformalized goal is incorrect, unprovable, or harder than the intended informal problem, so the failure need not indicate a prover shortcoming.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For the end-to-end pipeline, human experts judge semantic faithfulness, and the final derived theorem is compared with the original problem statement.

confounds.name: Reported model performance may reflect miniF2F data contamination
confounds.detail: The authors hypothesize that performance declines for Herald and Kimina on corrected versions may indicate that their v1 results benefit from contamination.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare autoformalization accuracy across v1 and v2 versions, noting that Herald and Kimina decline while o4-mini improves; they describe this as suggestive, not as a direct contamination test.

evidence_standards.name: Sampling budgets and evaluation settings
evidence_standards.detail: Specialized autoformalizers are evaluated at @1 or @128; at @128, human evaluation covers only the first translation that successfully passes the Lean compiler. o4-mini uses up to @10 with compiler feedback and stops at the first successful compilation. Theorem provers use @32.

evidence_standards.name: Human verification standard
evidence_standards.detail: Translations are manually verified by Lean experts; the paper reports both LLM-based and human-verified results. No seeds, variance summaries, statistical tests, or numerical threshold for calling a difference real are specified.

Models receive the full preceding in-file context. Main results use pass@128: a problem counts as solved if at least one of 128 generated attempts yields a successful proof.

metrics.caveat: The authors note that pass@128 is limited relative to larger sampling budgets and likely underestimates achievable performance; they also report scaling trends across k.

metrics.name: Proof length (lines of code)
metrics.caveat: Treated as a proxy for theorem complexity; the paper reports its correlation with model performance and compares successful model-generated proof lengths with human-written proof lengths.

confounds.name: Possible training-data contamination
confounds.detail: Contamination could inflate model scores without demonstrating genuine generalization to the benchmark theorems; the authors say contamination is unclear for models released after the projects’ first commits.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors note that Llemma 7B predates the projects’ first commits, making leakage impossible for that model. They do not rule out contamination for the other models.

confounds.name: Full in-file context may disadvantage theorem-proving models
confounds.detail: The full preceding file context may disadvantage NTP models trained on self-contained theorems, potentially contributing to low scores independently of research-level reasoning difficulty.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in these experiments; the authors identify it as a limitation and suggest investigating context retrieval or filtering.

confounds.name: Informal proofs may be cryptic without broader project context
confounds.detail: Cryptic informal proofs could limit the measured benefit of proof autoformalization, independently of models’ ability to use informative informal reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out in these experiments; the authors acknowledge this limitation and suggest providing additional context.

evidence_standards.name: Pass@128 sampling budget
evidence_standards.detail: Main results use 128 generated attempts per theorem; pass@k counts a theorem as solved if at least one of k attempts produces a successful proof. The paper also plots proof-autoformalization results across multiple k values. No seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported.

metrics.caveat: A well-formed Lean statement is not necessarily a correct formalization; the paper reports accuracy alongside it and notes that roughly half of Code-davinci-002's typechecking generations are correct. Copies of a formal statement from the prompt are excluded.

metrics.name: Formalization accuracy
metrics.caveat: Correctness is judged by a human expert because there is no general automatic way to verify equivalence of statements that are not definitionally equal.

metrics.name: Informalization accuracy

metrics.name: BLEU

The paper also notes that formalization BLEU may be higher because natural-language statements have more lexically distinct but semantically equivalent forms.

confounds.name: Data contamination from Mathematics in Lean

Models are evaluated on the validation set during experiments and once on the held-out test set at the end.

controls.name: Raw set.mm training data without synthetic augmentation
controls.detail: Compared with the augmented training dataset in the augmentation ablation.
controls.rules_out: Whether the reported augmentation uplift requires adding synthetically generated proofs.

controls.name: Policy-only training
controls.detail: Adds newly found positive proofs to policy training but does not train a value function; compared with policy+value.
controls.rules_out: Whether the iterative policy+value improvement is attributable to training the value function rather than adding positive proofs alone.

controls.name: GitHub-only additional pre-training
controls.detail: Continues CommonCrawl pre-training on GitHub alone for the same number of tokens as WebMath pre-training.
controls.rules_out: Whether WebMath's advantage over CommonCrawl is explained simply by additional pre-training tokens or GitHub data alone.

controls.name: CommonCrawl pre-training
controls.detail: Compared with models continued on WebMath, which starts from a CommonCrawl-pre-trained model.
controls.rules_out: Whether the gains attributed to WebMath require the WebMath continuation rather than generic CommonCrawl pre-training.

confounds.name: Synthetic augmentation gains could reflect memorization of generated training examples
confounds.detail: An apparent improvement on synthetic tasks could occur without the generators' proofs generalizing to new statements.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate on 100 synthetic statements different from the training set and report their proof rates.

confounds.name: WebMath gains could come from shallow syntactic features rather than more elaborate reasoning-relevant features
confounds.detail: The headline pre-training improvement could occur through transfer of mostly syntactic features, without the claimed broader relevance to formal reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare with GitHub-only pre-training: it performs worse than WebMath. The paper presents this as suggestive evidence, while leaving a broader investigation to future work.

confounds.name: Overfitting could distort iterative training and its reported performance
confounds.detail: The authors hypothesize that overfitting makes exploration collapse because the model is overly optimistic about training-set predictions.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Track loss on the associated validation set and early-stop at minimum validation loss.

evidence_standards.name: Proof-search decoding settings
evidence_standards.detail: For model evaluations, use e=32 sampled tactics per expansion and d=128 expansions; validation evaluations generally use a=4 attempts per statement. The final test evaluation uses e=32, d=256, and a=32.

evidence_standards.name: Variance and interpreting differences
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says a=4 limits evaluation variance while remaining tractable, and that increasing attempts decreases variance. It describes the 160m raw-versus-augmented difference as within typical variance and calls the larger-model augmentation effect more reliably positive. It reports no seed count, confidence interval, or statistical test.

datasets.name: PutnamBench
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated separately by language: 640 Lean 4 formalizations, 640 Isabelle formalizations, and 412 Coq formalizations. No train/test split is specified. A proof counts as successful when accepted by the formal proof environment; results are reported as solved problems over the number of formalizations. The paper uses method-specific attempt budgets and settings, including pass@10 for GPT-4 and DSP, and pass@1 with 60 GPT-4 queries for COPRA.

baselines.name: GPT-4
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper says evaluations across languages use GPT-4o with in-context examples and describes the Isabelle and Coq runs as using the same configuration as Lean, with language-specific prompts.

controls.name: ReProver without retrieval
controls.detail: The authors evaluate ReProver with the retrieval component held out, alongside the version with retrieval.
controls.rules_out: A difference between the two conditions would indicate whether retrieval contributes to ReProver's results; both conditions solve 0 of 640 problems.

confounds.name: Direct contamination from existing formal Putnam proofs
confounds.detail: Previously produced formal proofs could make benchmark problems easier without demonstrating new theorem-proving ability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors searched formal mathematics repositories for Lean, Isabelle, and Coq and found no aligned Putnam theorems and proofs; they also do not include formal proofs in the benchmark.

confounds.name: Indirect contamination through training on informal Putnam proofs
confounds.detail: Transfer from informal proofs in training data could contribute to performance without the model independently solving the formal problem.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by a reported measurement; the authors acknowledge that indirect contamination can occur.

evidence_standards.name: Formal proof acceptance
evidence_standards.detail: A successful result is determined by whether the formal proof environment accepts the proof.

evidence_standards.name: Reported generation and search settings
evidence_standards.detail: GPT-4 uses pass@10 at temperature 0.7; DSP uses pass@10 at temperature 0.1. COPRA uses pass@1 with 60 GPT-4 queries (temperature 0.0 is specified for Coq). Sledgehammer has a 120-second timeout; Tactician has a 600-second per-problem timeout; CoqHammer has 120 seconds total per formalization.

evidence_standards.name: No reported uncertainty or statistical testing
evidence_standards.detail: The authors report no error bars; results are presented as raw solved-problem counts, with no seed-based variance estimates or statistical tests.

datasets.name: Metamath set.mm
datasets.eval_protocol: Random theorem train/validation/test split, with 1,000 theorems each in validation and test; the dependency DAG prevents validation or test theorems from being used to prove another theorem. Reports pass@8 and pass@32; validation also has cumulative pass rate during online training.

datasets.name: miniF2F-valid
datasets.eval_protocol: In the transductive setup, statements are used during online training and cumulative pass rate is reported; the paper also reports pass@64. In the earlier setup, validation is evaluated as an unseen split.

datasets.name: miniF2F-test
datasets.eval_protocol: Held-out test split; reports pass@64 for Lean results and, in the Metamath/Lean experiment tables as applicable, pass@k using the stated number of proof searches.

datasets.name: miniF2F-curriculum
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as online-training statements in the Lean experiments; statements were sampled on average 250 times each after one day. Reports cumulative pass rate when evaluated during training and pass@64.

datasets.name: Identities
datasets.eval_protocol: A manually created out-of-domain set of 160 mathematical expressions in Equations, used for online training and evaluation; reports cumulative pass rate.

baselines.name: GPT-f
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same named Lean and Metamath evaluation sets. The abstract describes the miniF2F-curriculum comparison as using a similar computational budget; no other matched conditions are specified.

baselines.name: Supervised model
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares against its supervised-only model; for the repeated-attempt comparison, it uses the same number of proof attempts.

metrics.name: Cumulative pass rate
metrics.caveat: On transductive splits it counts theorems solved at least once during online training, so those statements have been available during training; the paper also reports pass@k on evaluation statements, including held-out test results.

controls.name: Supervised model with the same number of proof attempts
controls.detail: Runs proof attempts without online learning from previous searches, compared with the online-trained model.
controls.rules_out: That the improvement is explained solely by making more attempts on the statements.

controls.name: No critic
controls.detail: Search is guided by the policy alone; leaf values are set to 0.5 and there is no critic training objective.
controls.rules_out: That the reported improvement requires no contribution from the critic.

controls.name: Hard critic
controls.detail: Critic targets are 1 for solved nodes and 0 for invalid and internal nodes.
controls.rules_out: That the benefit is independent of the paper's soft internal-node critic targets.

controls.name: Fixed proof-search parameters
controls.detail: Uses chosen fixed HTPS hyperparameters instead of sampling them for each attempt.
controls.rules_out: That stochastic search-parameter sampling is unnecessary for the reported gains.

controls.name: Slower or absent model updates
controls.detail: Compares updates every 5 minutes with updates every 1 hour or 6 hours, and with no updates in the stated experiments.
controls.rules_out: That frequent model refresh during online training makes no difference.

controls.name: Alternative tactic-training sample selection
controls.detail: Tests all-node policy samples and samples from all proofs or minimal proofs of solved nodes or of the root theorem.
controls.rules_out: That the reported result is unaffected by which proof-search data is selected for tactic training.

controls.name: Lean without synthetic-data co-training
controls.detail: Removes the synthetic Equations-generated theorem co-training task.
controls.rules_out: That the synthetic co-training task is not contributing to the reported Lean performance.

confounds.name: Improvement comes from repeated attempts rather than learning from proof searches
confounds.detail: The headline gain on statements used during online training could arise simply because they received many more proof attempts.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare against a supervised model given the same number of attempts; the paper reports that online training performs better on Metamath and Equations.

evidence_standards.name: Pass@k proof-search trial counts
evidence_standards.detail: Reports results under k proof searches per evaluated statement, using pass@8, pass@32, or pass@64 in the stated experiments. The paper does not report seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: ProofNetVerif
datasets.eval_protocol: 3,752 formal-informal examples with human-annotated binary semantic-equivalence labels; reports BEqL and BEq+ precision, recall, and F1. The metrics were evaluated once and not tuned on this dataset; no split is stated.

datasets.name: ProofNet#
datasets.eval_protocol: Corrected Lean 4 version of ProofNet; 118 formalization errors in the Lean 4 ports were corrected. Sampling-method ablations use the validation split and 12-shot prompting. Final comparisons report greedy decoding against sampling at T=0.7 with n=50; the split for those final results is not stated. Reports manual accuracy and symbolic metrics.

datasets.name: RLM25
datasets.eval_protocol: 619 natural-language/Lean pairs from six research-level formalization projects. No train/test split is stated. Evaluations include statement-only input, in-file context, and context ablations; final results use in-file context with proofs removed. Lean REPL is used for evaluation, with support backported to the projects’ Lean versions.

baselines.name: Greedy decoding
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with sampling-based methods on the same models and benchmarks; ProofNet# uses 12-shot prompting, and the sampled method uses T=0.7 and n=50. RLM25 uses in-file context with proofs removed.

baselines.name: Random selection
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other selection heuristics on the same sampled candidates; the selection-method study applies type-check filtering before selection.

baselines.name: Majority voting
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other selection heuristics on the same sampled candidates; the selection-method study applies type-check filtering before selection.

baselines.name: Self-BLEU
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other selection heuristics on the same sampled candidates; the selection-method study applies type-check filtering before selection.

baselines.name: Symbolic equivalence selection
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with other selection heuristics on the same sampled candidates and type-check filtering; its evaluation is limited to n≤50 because of computational cost.

baselines.name: MMA fine-tuning
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with few-shot/base-model approaches on RLM25; further matching details are not stated.

baselines.name: Lean Workbook fine-tuning
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with few-shot/base-model approaches on RLM25; further matching details are not stated.

metrics.name: Type-check rate
metrics.caveat: Its correlation with human accuracy is relatively low, so the paper says it cannot substitute for human evaluation; it reports human accuracy alongside it and suggests it may approximate accuracy when comparing experiments for a single model.

metrics.name: BEq+
metrics.caveat: It is conservative relative to human accuracy and has lower recall on long statements (29.6%, versus 62.5% on short statements); the paper compares it with human annotations and reports precision/recall on ProofNetVerif.

metrics.name: BEqL
metrics.caveat: It has a relatively high false-negative rate; the paper reports precision and recall on ProofNetVerif and compares benchmark-level scores with human accuracy.

metrics.name: pass@n
metrics.caveat: It measures whether at least one of n outputs is correct and is reported as the score achievable with a perfect selector, so it is an oracle upper bound rather than a selection method’s achieved score.

metrics.name: Precision
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside recall and F1 for metric evaluation on ProofNetVerif.

metrics.name: Recall
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside precision and F1 for metric evaluation on ProofNetVerif.

metrics.name: F1 score
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside precision and recall for metric evaluation on ProofNetVerif.

metrics.name: Pearson correlation
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside Kendall correlation for agreement between automated metrics and human accuracy.

metrics.name: Kendall correlation
metrics.caveat: Reported alongside Pearson correlation for agreement between automated metrics and human accuracy.

controls.name: No type-check filter with random selection
controls.detail: Sampling candidates are selected randomly without filtering; compared with filtered sampling conditions in the filtering ablation.
controls.rules_out: That the observed improvement is due to sampling and selection alone rather than the type-check filter.

controls.name: No type-check filter with majority voting
controls.detail: Majority voting is applied to sampled candidates without type-check filtering.
controls.rules_out: That majority voting without the filter explains the gains attributed to the filtered sampling pipeline.

controls.name: No type-check filter with Self-BLEU
controls.detail: Self-BLEU selects from sampled candidates without type-check filtering.
controls.rules_out: That Self-BLEU selection without the filter explains the gains attributed to the filtered sampling pipeline.

controls.name: Type-check filter with random selection
controls.detail: Candidates are filtered for well-typedness and then selected randomly.
controls.rules_out: That the gains require a particular final selection heuristic rather than type-check filtering.

controls.name: Greedy decoding
controls.detail: The standard greedy-decoding result is compared with the sampled, filtered method.
controls.rules_out: That the reported sampling-based improvement is merely the model’s ordinary greedy-decoding performance.

controls.name: RLM25 statement-only input
controls.detail: The natural-language statement is provided without in-file context; compared with prompts containing file context.
controls.rules_out: That research-level results with context reflect performance achievable from the statement alone.

controls.name: RLM25 context with proofs removed
controls.detail: File context is retained except for proofs; compared with full file context and other context ablations.
controls.rules_out: That the contextual performance improvement depends on including proof text.

controls.name: RLM25 context with theorems and proofs removed
controls.detail: Both theorems and proofs are removed from the file context.
controls.rules_out: That the measured contextual effect is unaffected by which file components are available.

confounds.name: Data contamination in RLM25
confounds.detail: Models might have encountered benchmark material during training, which could explain their performance without demonstrating generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors report that project first-commit dates postdate the evaluated models’ announced knowledge cutoffs and say their additional contamination study found contamination unlikely.

confounds.name: Missing file context, rather than model capability, explains poor research-level results
confounds.detail: Without local definitions, opened namespaces, and local variables, models may lack information needed to formalize the statements; poor statement-only scores would not by themselves show inability to formalize with appropriate context.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They evaluate RLM25 with in-file context and ablate context components, including removing proofs and removing both theorems and proofs. The results show substantial gains with context and the best performance with proofs removed.

confounds.name: Incorrect reference formalizations bias benchmark evaluation
confounds.detail: Errors in the Lean 4 ports of ProofNet could distort downstream evaluation against reference formalizations.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors identify and correct 118 erroneous entries (31.8% of the entries), producing ProofNet#.

confounds.name: Symbolic equivalence metrics miss semantically equivalent formalizations
confounds.detail: False negatives could make automated metric scores understate correctness, especially for long statements.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They compare BEqL and BEq+ with human labels on ProofNetVerif and compare benchmark-level metric scores with human accuracy; they also measure the length effect, finding BEq+ recall falls from 62.5% on short statements to 29.6% on long statements, so this limitation is quantified but not eliminated.

confounds.name: Equivalence checking could use unrelated library theorems and falsely accept a candidate
confounds.detail: The exact? tactic could prove a statement using an unrelated true theorem, making two unrelated formalizations appear equivalent.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For BEqL, exact? is restricted to use only the candidate equivalent formula.

evidence_standards.name: Manual accuracy uses semantic-equivalence judgments
evidence_standards.detail: Accuracy is defined as the proportion of statements judged correct by manual annotation, where correct means semantically equivalent to the natural-language statement. The paper does not state a statistical significance test, seed count, or variance-reporting rule.

evidence_standards.name: Sampling and decoding conditions
evidence_standards.detail: Unless otherwise stated, sampling uses temperature T=0.7 and n=50 attempts per statement. ProofNet# uses 12-shot prompting; final RLM25 results use in-file context with proofs removed. Sampling ablations are conducted on the ProofNet# validation split.

evidence_standards.name: ProofNetVerif metric evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: BEqL and BEq+ are evaluated once on ProofNetVerif, and their designs are not tuned to that dataset.

datasets.name: miniF2F
datasets.eval_protocol: Use the 244-problem test split. For global perturbations, evaluate each problem in Orig plus G-FF, Q-FF, G-Step, and Q-Step styles. For local perturbations, create one edit per problem for each applicable edit-type/location combination; include only cases with an eligible location.

datasets.name: MATH-500
datasets.eval_protocol: Use all 500 problems; append each gold answer to the statement as a “Show that it is X” clause to make it a proposition requiring proof, and use the reference solution as the informal proof. Evaluate five input styles for global perturbations and one edit per problem for each applicable local edit-type/location combination, only where an eligible location exists.

baselines.name: Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout; model-specific decoding settings are used.

baselines.name: Kimina-Prover-Distill-8B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout; model-specific decoding settings are used.

baselines.name: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout; model-specific decoding settings are used.

baselines.name: Goedel-Prover-V2-8B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout; model-specific decoding settings are used.

baselines.name: Gemini-3.1-Pro
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout; model-specific decoding settings are used.

baselines.name: ProofBridge
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout. Uses the SFT model trained with released code; the retrieval component is not included.

baselines.name: ProofFlow
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated on the same benchmark inputs with one output per input, the same semantic/faithfulness judge, and Lean 4 type checking with a 900-second per-problem timeout; model-specific decoding settings are used.

metrics.name: Type Correctness (TC)
metrics.caveat: Lean accepts outputs containing sorry with a warning rather than an error; the authors note such outputs are rare among inspected FullyCorrect outputs.

metrics.name: Statement Semantic Correctness (StmtSC)
metrics.caveat: Assigned by an LLM judge, so judge-specific bias is a concern; the paper also validates labels with a second judge and manual inspection.

metrics.name: Proof Semantic Correctness (ProofSC)
metrics.caveat: Assigned by an LLM judge, so judge-specific bias is a concern; the paper also validates labels with a second judge and manual inspection.

metrics.name: FullyCorrect
metrics.caveat: Requires TC, StmtSC, and ProofSC all to pass; TC can accept outputs containing sorry.

metrics.name: Faithful Rate (FR)
metrics.caveat: Computed only over identifiable outputs (faithful or reverted), excluding unclear outputs; the paper reports Unclear Rate alongside it.

metrics.name: Reverted Rate (RR)
metrics.caveat: Computed only over identifiable outputs (faithful or reverted), excluding unclear outputs; the paper reports Unclear Rate alongside it.

confounds.name: The constructed perturbations may change more than the intended content or fail to preserve meaning
confounds.detail: If edits alter unintended spans, or paraphrases change mathematical content, model results would not isolate robustness to the specified perturbation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Character-by-character comparison found exactly one intended contiguous changed span in all 2,637 local edits. For global perturbations, automated checks found 96.4% preserved all numeric and symbolic tokens (the remainder differed only in formatting), and manual inspection of 100 stratified pairs found meaning and reasoning preserved.

confounds.name: Semantic-label results may be specific to the Gemini-2.5-Flash judge
confounds.detail: A judge-specific bias could make the reported StmtSC and ProofSC differences reflect its judgments rather than model behavior.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Re-judged 200 global-experiment outputs with GPT-5.4-mini: agreement was 88.5% for StmtSC and 84.5% for ProofSC, with Cohen’s kappa 0.735 and 0.690. Manual checks of 100 verdicts per metric agreed with the judge on 94 StmtSC and 90 ProofSC cases.

confounds.name: High step-deletion faithfulness for Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B may reflect inability to produce proofs rather than genuine retention of the deleted gap
confounds.detail: Its empty proof bodies count as faithful, so limited proof-generation ability could inflate FR without showing that the model preserves missing reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Recomputed FR excluding empty proof bodies: it falls to 12.9% on miniF2F and 39.6% on MATH-500; no model then exceeds 40%.

confounds.name: Differences between models may reflect size and training data rather than the model approach
confounds.detail: The paper explicitly notes that the models are run in available configurations and that cross-model differences also reflect model size and training data.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper acknowledges this as a limitation.

evidence_standards.name: Main evaluation decoding and output count
evidence_standards.detail: The reported main results use one output per input. Appendix D additionally evaluates eight sampled outputs per input and reports that style has a small but consistent effect beyond sampling. No seed count, statistical test, variance interval, or numerical no-difference margin is specified.

evidence_standards.name: Judge reliability checks
evidence_standards.detail: For semantic-label validation, the paper re-judges 200 outputs with a second judge and manually checks 100 verdicts per metric. For number and symbol faithfulness labels, the judge’s verdict matches the value reported from the output in 96.7% of 16,212 cases.

datasets.name: MG200
datasets.eval_protocol: 200 informal geometry problems: 43 historical IMO, 77 LeanGeo-Bench non-IMO, 22 CertiGeo, and 58 OMNI-Geometry problems. GeoFormalizer is evaluated on these problems; GeoProver is evaluated on the Lean statements it produces. RQ1 reports successful elaboration counts and percentages; RQ2 uses the Claude Opus 4.8-generated statements and reports kernel-checked proof counts, with proof/refutation/timeout outcomes also reported for GPT-5.6-Sol.

datasets.name: IMO geometry problems (historical, 43)
datasets.eval_protocol: GeoFormalizer elaboration is evaluated across seven backbones. In RQ3, statements are formalized with Claude Opus 4.8 and proved with GPT-5.6-Sol; GeoProver proves 29, refutes 14, and proves all 14 after expert repair.

datasets.name: LeanGeo-Bench (77 non-IMO problems)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as the 77-problem LeanGeo non-IMO subset of MG200 for autoformalization; successful Lean elaboration is reported by model and method.

datasets.name: CertiGeo (22 classical geometry theorems)
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as the 22-problem CertiGeo subset of MG200 to evaluate autoformalization and algebraic proving; successful Lean elaboration is reported by model and method.

datasets.name: OMNI-Geometry (58 problems)
datasets.eval_protocol: 58 plane geometry problems sampled by difficulty are used as the OMNI-Geometry subset of MG200 for autoformalization; successful Lean elaboration is reported by model and method.

datasets.name: PutnamBench
datasets.eval_protocol: 31 selected Lean plane Euclidean geometry statements based on EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2); GeoProver and comparison provers are evaluated on them, reporting kernel-checked proof counts. Provers receive a two-hour per-problem budget except Goedel-Prover-V2-8B, which uses its original pass@32 protocol.

datasets.name: Lean-IMO-Bench (14 geometry problems)
datasets.eval_protocol: All 14 geometry problems are evaluated. In RQ3, GeoFormalizer uses Claude Opus 4.8 and GeoProver uses GPT-5.6-Sol; the paper reports proofs, verified refutations, and proofs after human repair.

datasets.name: IMO 2026 Problem 2
datasets.eval_protocol: Formalized directly from the informal problem and proved by GeoProver; one proof is reported.

baselines.name: Direct translation
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same LLM backbones and problem sets as GeoFormalizer; it makes a single translation attempt.

baselines.name: Euclean
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the autoformalization datasets across the reported model backbones. The paper notes settings differ: Euclean receives a 10-minute timeout and made 14–116 model calls per problem in these runs, while GeoFormalizer uses at most five calls.

baselines.name: Numina-Lean-Agent
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same DeepSeek-V4-Pro backend, input statements, and two-hour per-problem budget as GeoProver; the default official-release prompt is retained.

baselines.name: Hilbert
baselines.fair_comparison: Uses the same DeepSeek-V4-Pro backend, input statements, and two-hour per-problem budget as GeoProver; the default official-release prompt is retained.

baselines.name: Goedel-Prover-V2-8B
baselines.fair_comparison: Evaluated with its released 8B model using pass@32, following its original evaluation protocol; the paper does not claim the same backend or budget as GeoProver.

metrics.name: Successful elaboration rate
metrics.caveat: Lean acceptance establishes syntactic and type correctness, not that the statement captures the intended theorem; the paper also reports semantic consistency.

metrics.name: Semantic consistency
metrics.caveat: Human inspection can miss degeneracy and order errors; the paper also uses formal counterexample search and reports proof, refutation, and timeout outcomes.

metrics.name: Kernel-checked proof success
metrics.caveat: Proving a formal statement does not establish that it faithfully represents the informal problem; the paper cross-tabulates outcomes with semantic judgments and reports formal refutations and repaired-statement proofs.

metrics.name: Formal refutation count
metrics.caveat: A refutation concerns the formal statement and may expose a mismatch with the intended problem; the paper reports the counterexample and, where applicable, expert-repaired proofs.

metrics.name: F score
metrics.caveat: The score combines semantic and structural signals; the paper reports the judge and structural components, and accepts candidates at F ≥ 0.6.

metrics.name: Semantic judge score (S_judge)
metrics.caveat: It can be ambiguous between partial consistency and other judgments; the paper also uses structural point coverage, which is decisive when S_judge = 0.5.

metrics.name: Structural score (S_struct; point coverage ratio)
metrics.caveat: It measures only the fraction of GeoIR-declared points mentioned in the informal problem; the paper combines it with the semantic judge score rather than using it alone.

controls.name: GeoFormalizer repair-round ablations
controls.detail: Compare settings (0,0), (0,2), (2,0), and (2,2), where the entries are compiler-guided and semantic-guided repair rounds; all other reported evaluation setup is held fixed.
controls.rules_out: Whether the elaboration gains require repair, and the separate contribution of compiler-guided versus semantic-guided repair.

controls.name: GeoProver without external CAS
controls.detail: Remove external computer algebra systems while keeping the other components, including the DeepSeek-V4-Pro backbone, unchanged.
controls.rules_out: That the full system’s proof results arise without a contribution from external symbolic computation.

controls.name: GeoProver without CAS and without the algebraization toolkit
controls.detail: Remove both external CAS and the Lean-side algebraization toolkit; other components remain unchanged.
controls.rules_out: Whether algebraization provides value beyond external CAS, including as an intermediate representation for Lean reasoning.

confounds.name: A formal theorem may be unfaithful to the informal problem
confounds.detail: A proof can succeed on an unintended formalization, so proof success alone could look like solving the source geometry problem when it has not.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper separately evaluates semantic consistency, cross-tabulates human judgments with proof/refutation outcomes, and uses Lean-verified counterexamples; it also reports proofs after expert repair.

confounds.name: Human semantic review may miss implicit nondegeneracy or order conditions
confounds.detail: A statement judged faithful by people may admit degenerate or wrongly ordered configurations, allowing a counterexample despite the intended theorem being true.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Formal counterexample search and Lean-verified counterexamples; the paper reports that this refuted 22 statements initially judged faithful and describes repaired examples.

confounds.name: Elaboration improvements may not reflect semantic improvements
confounds.detail: A Lean statement can elaborate successfully while expressing an inconsistent, trivial, or otherwise different theorem.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports semantic evaluation separately from elaboration, including expert majority judgments on 200 Claude Opus 4.8 statements and semantic-guided repair.

confounds.name: Proof gains might come solely from LLM-based proof search rather than the algebraic components
confounds.detail: The full system’s proof count could otherwise be attributed to the LLM prover without a contribution from CAS or the algebraization interface.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Ablations remove CAS and then both CAS and the algebraization toolkit while holding other components, including the backbone, unchanged; proof counts decrease in both conditions.

evidence_standards.name: Three-expert semantic annotation with majority vote
evidence_standards.detail: Three experts independently assess the 200 statements generated by Claude Opus 4.8; a statement is accepted only by majority vote, using criteria covering objects, constructions, hypotheses, admissible configurations, and conclusion.

evidence_standards.name: Per-problem proving budget
evidence_standards.detail: RQ2 provers receive a two-hour budget per problem in a sandbox. RQ3 reports 28 historical IMO statements proved within two hours and one additional statement proved in 2 hours and 6 minutes.

evidence_standards.name: Goedel-Prover-V2-8B decoding protocol
evidence_standards.detail: Reported using pass@32 following its original evaluation protocol.

evidence_standards.name: Kernel-checked outcomes

A proof attempt counts as successful only if the target ITP verifies it and it contains no fake proofs such as admit or sorry. Models use pass@n: GPT-o4-mini-high gets one attempt per problem; other models get 8 attempts, with pass@1, pass@4, and pass@8 reported where available. Hammers are reported at pass@1. Each verification attempt has a 10-minute timeout.

controls.detail: The downstream proof workflow gives the prover only the goal and uses the same fixed prover/reflection workflow as retrieval conditions.

controls.name: LeanSearch v2 retriever-only
controls.detail: The MathlibQR ablation removes the Qwen3-Reranker-8B stage from LeanSearch v2’s retrieve-rerank pipeline.
controls.rules_out: That the full system’s search result is explained without a contribution from reranking.

controls.name: No-reflection reasoning loop
controls.detail: An ablation of reasoning mode removes the reflection loop; the paper reports an ablation against this variant in Appendix D.3.
controls.rules_out: That the reasoning-mode result does not depend on reflection.

controls.name: Without kind-aware prompting
controls.detail: The standard-mode step-wise ablation compares the kind-aware prompting design with a version without that design.
controls.rules_out: That the definition-retrieval gain from kind-aware prompting is explained by the rest of the retrieval pipeline alone.

confounds.name: Mathlib snapshot drift
confounds.detail: A system could appear better because its snapshot contains more ground-truth declarations, rather than because it retrieves better.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The main MathlibQR comparison uses the 810 query rows whose ground-truth declarations exist in every system’s snapshot, on the shared 171-declaration corpus subset.

confounds.name: Position bias in LLM judgments
confounds.detail: The LLM judge’s system ordering could reflect presentation position rather than retrieval quality.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Top-5 results are presented in three independent random permutations per query; the paper also reports position-bias and cross-round-agreement diagnostics, including a primacy-bias correction.

evidence_standards.name: LLM-judge repetitions
evidence_standards.detail: Claude Sonnet 4.5 judges three independent random permutations per query; the paper reports mean rank over 2,430 judgments per system and provides position-bias and cross-round-agreement diagnostics.

evidence_standards.name: Fixed downstream proof workflow
evidence_standards.detail: All configurations use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as prover and reflection LLM, with 8 reflection rounds; a problem counts as solved only with a Lean-verified, sorry-free proof. The paper does not report seeds or a statistical significance test.

datasets.name: MathlibQR

metrics.name: pass@k
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that pass@32 alone can make gains less apparent; it also reports pass rates at smaller reflection budgets, including 8 and 16 turns.

metrics.name: API cost per solved problem
metrics.caveat: The calculation includes API expenditure from unsuccessful runs and divides by the number of problems solved within 32 turns; lower values indicate better cost efficiency.

controls.name: No retrieval
controls.detail: The vanilla backbone LLM runs without retrieval alongside the retrieval configurations.
controls.rules_out: Provides a no-retrieval reference for whether retrieval conditions improve proof completion and cost.

controls.name: Failure memory disabled
controls.detail: The proving configurations are evaluated both with failure memory disabled and enabled.
controls.rules_out: Shows whether observed results depend on adding the paper’s failure-memory mechanism.

confounds.name: Retrieval gains come merely from expanding the retrieved context
confounds.detail: A larger context could appear to improve retrieval by including more declarations, without concentrating useful premises.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On MathlibMPR, the paper reports that LeanGraphSearch returns fewer filtered declarations on average than LeanSearch v2 while retrieving more gold declarations within the top five.

evidence_standards.name: Reported proving budgets and backbone setting
evidence_standards.detail: Report pass rates at 8, 16, and 32 reflection turns, with at most 32 turns and one optional query per turn; use Gemini 3.1 Pro as the prover backbone and fix the prompt, verifier, action budget, and model settings across configurations.

evidence_standards.name: Two-backbone averaging for MathlibMPR retrieval comparison

datasets.name: miniF2F
datasets.eval_protocol: Run corpus-scale Lean 4 static checkers over released variants: v2c, v2s, yangky11, yangky11-early, justincasher, harmonic, and ai-mo (488 problems per variant except justincasher and harmonic at 485 and ai-mo at 244); forks and variants are counted separately, not deduplicated. datasets.eval_protocol: Run corpus-scale Lean 4 static checkers on the hf variant (100 problems). The semantic-audit challenge set contains 34 problems from CombiBench; each is assessed in six error categories.

A 55-example labeled warning-verification set is used to evaluate LLM filtering of checker warnings. The semantic-audit challenge set contains 23 problems from ProverBench, each assessed in six error categories. ProverBench is also included in the 20-problem mechanically proven-issue correction study across four datasets; no per-dataset allocation is given.

metrics.name: Static-checker findings
metrics.caveat: Findings are audit signals, not all confirmed defects; the authors caution that counts across forks and ports are not deduplicated and should not be interpreted as benchmark-level error rates.

metrics.name: Proven issues
metrics.caveat: Counts only findings with a machine-checkable certificate of unprovability or vacuity; semantic equivalence still requires human adjudication.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: For warning verification, the paper says the LLM-assisted process is not foolproof; Gemini 3.0 Flash has the highest reported accuracy (83.3%).

metrics.name: Precision
metrics.caveat: Semantic-audit precision is low (0.30 for Sonnet 4.5 + Thinking and 0.24 for GPT-5.2 + Thinking); the authors say human filtering of false positives is needed.

metrics.name: Recall
metrics.caveat: High recall does not by itself make semantic-audit outputs reliable because precision is low; the paper recommends human verification.

metrics.name: F1
metrics.caveat: Reported across the six semantic error types, with substantially weaker performance on formalization errors than on specification errors and definition mismatches.

metrics.name: Pass rate
metrics.caveat: Defects can inflate or deflate prover scores, and the opposing effects can coexist and partially cancel; the authors warn that headline pass rates are unreliable without per-item quality audits.

metrics.name: Solved count
metrics.caveat: On the selected 20 mechanically proven-issue problems, both provers solved 0/20 flawed statements, but solved items after correction; the paper explains that such flawed items can silently deflate scores.

controls.name: Original statements alongside manually corrected statements
controls.detail: The same evaluated prover checkpoints were run on original and manually corrected versions of 20 problems selected for mechanically proven issues across four datasets.
controls.rules_out: That the reported change in solved count is merely a difference between prover checkpoints; it shows that correcting defective statements can change measured scores.

controls.name: ProofNet alongside its human-corrected counterpart ProofNet#
controls.detail: The paper compares measured prover pass rates on ProofNet and the repaired ProofNet# statements.
controls.rules_out: That the weaker original formalizations leave measured pass rates unchanged; the paper reports lower pass rates after repairing weakened statements.

confounds.name: Checker warnings may be false positives because the static checker misses guards
confounds.detail: A guard may be present in a form the checker cannot recognize, such as inside a structure definition, a subtype constraint, or a non-local invariant, so a warning need not indicate a real defect.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For dagger-marked warning categories, an LLM checks surrounding code context. On a labeled 55-example ProverBench warning-verification set, the paper reports accuracy, precision, and recall; on ProverBench filtering reduced findings by 35% while preserving all confirmed true positives.

confounds.name: Semantic-audit LLMs may flag errors that are not present
confounds.detail: The semantic detectors have low precision, so apparent detection performance could reflect false positives rather than reliable identification of mismatches.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate against ground-truth labels on a curated challenge set and report precision, recall, F1, and accuracy; the results show low precision, and the authors state that human filtering remains necessary.

confounds.name: Corpus-wide finding totals may overstate independent defects because variants overlap
confounds.detail: Forks, ports, and subsets of the same benchmarks are counted separately, so repeated findings need not represent distinct benchmark problems.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out: the paper explicitly says Table 4 is not deduplicated and its counts should not be read as benchmark-level error rates.

metrics.name: Testing Accuracy (TA)
metrics.caveat: Passing successor compilation is evidence, not a guarantee, of semantic correctness; few successors may miss errors, and even many successors cannot guarantee completeness. The paper reports TA alongside compilation accuracy and analyzes its change with successor coverage.

metrics.name: Compilation accuracy
metrics.caveat: Compilation in isolation does not establish semantic correctness and substantially overestimates it; the paper reports TA alongside it and reports compilation’s precision as a predictor of semantic correctness as 6.89%.

metrics.name: BLEU
metrics.caveat: Lexical similarity does not reliably indicate semantic correctness: over 70% of samples in the 90–100 BLEU bins are testing-incorrect, while about 30% in the 0–10 bins are testing-verified. The paper compares BLEU bins against testing outcomes.

controls.name: Withhold successor theorem context
controls.detail: Compare the default NL-proof-plus-successor-theorem context against conditions with successor theorem context withheld, with and without the NL proof.
controls.rules_out: Whether providing successor theorems as generation context is responsible for the observed TA difference.

controls.name: Withhold NL proof context
controls.detail: Compare the default NL-proof-plus-successor-theorem context against conditions with the NL proof withheld, with and without successor theorem context.
controls.rules_out: Whether providing the NL proof as generation context is responsible for the observed TA difference.

confounds.name: High compilation accuracy may reflect syntactic or logical validity without semantic correctness
confounds.detail: If compilation were an adequate proxy for semantic correctness, high compilation scores could be interpreted as high semantic performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Measure TA alongside compilation accuracy; report that compilation’s precision as a predictor of semantic correctness is 6.89%.

confounds.name: Lexical similarity may be mistaken for semantic correctness
confounds.detail: If BLEU tracked intended meaning, high BLEU would indicate testing-verified theorems and low BLEU would indicate failures.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare testing outcomes across BLEU bins; over 70% of samples in the 90–100 bins are incorrect, and about 30% in the 0–10 bins are verified correct.

confounds.name: Low T2 Hard results may arise because models do not understand the task format, rather than inability to produce the intended formalization
confounds.detail: A format-understanding problem could make zero-shot performance low even if models can solve the task once shown examples.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate four top-performing models with two in-context examples sampled from Herald; the paper reports no consistent TA gain.

confounds.name: Generated NL specifications may be noisy because they were written by an LLM rather than the original theorem authors
confounds.detail: Annotation noise could affect autoformalization results independently of theorem-generation capability.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Manually verify 10 randomly sampled NL annotations; the paper reports finding no errors, while acknowledging this does not remove the limitation.

evidence_standards.name: Reported decoding setup
evidence_standards.detail: Model evaluations are reported in a zero-shot setting with temperature 0.6 and top_p 0.95. The paper does not report seeds, variance estimates, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

datasets.name: miniF2F
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the Lean version updated for Lean 4 and natural-language descriptions; 488 theorems total, split into 244 validation and 244 test theorems. Proof attempts are capped at 128 per theorem, proof length at 2048 tokens, and correctness is checked with Lean 4.13. For adaptive evaluation, selects 5 theorems per round and continues until the ability score changes by less than 0.01 for 10 consecutive rounds; reports the number of theorems used. Pass@N is also reported for comparison.

datasets.name: miniF2F-Graded
datasets.eval_protocol: The annotated 488-theorem Lean miniF2F dataset. Difficulty and discrimination are calculated using four annotation LLMs; the reported difficulty-level analysis uses four levels, with Level 4 containing theorems all annotation LLMs failed. Evaluation uses 128 attempts per theorem and Lean 4.13 verification; adaptive evaluation selects 5 theorems per round until the stated convergence criterion is met.

baselines.name: Pass@N evaluation (including Pass@128)
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper compares ability-score rankings and Pass@N rankings for the same evaluated LLMs; Pass@128 results are also reported alongside ability scores. No further equalization is stated.

baselines.name: Original miniF2F manual difficulty grading
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with miniF2F-Graded on the MATH-category theorems that have original manual grades, using model Pass@128 results across difficulty levels.

metrics.name: Pass@N
metrics.caveat: Treats theorems as equally important, so it can obscure performance disparities; the paper reports adaptive ability scores alongside it.

metrics.name: Ability Score
metrics.caveat: It is on a different scale from pass rates and cannot be directly compared numerically. The paper compares model rankings with Pass@16, Pass@32, Pass@64, and Pass@128 rankings; one model pair differs from the Pass@128 ranking.

metrics.name: Discrimination
metrics.caveat: A negative value may indicate data contamination or unusually strong performance by a lower-ability model, warranting investigation.

controls.name: Difficulty calculation without the correction term
controls.detail: The authors also calculate theorem difficulty without the correction term in the difficulty formula.
controls.rules_out: Comparing with this ablation tests whether the correction term helps distinguish theorem difficulty levels; the paper reports that including it makes the levels easier to distinguish.

confounds.name: The new difficulty grades may not reflect difficulty as perceived by LLMs, but instead reproduce human grading
confounds.detail: The paper notes that the original miniF2F difficulty levels were assigned manually and that human and LLM difficulty perceptions may differ.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares model Pass@128 rates across difficulty levels under miniF2F-Graded and the original miniF2F grading, including results for the shared MATH-category theorems.

confounds.name: Ability-score rankings may not reflect models’ theorem-proving ability
confounds.detail: The adaptive score is produced from a selected subset of theorems, so its rankings could differ from rankings using pass rates over the full dataset.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compares ability-score rankings with Pass@16, Pass@32, Pass@64, and Pass@128 rankings; the paper reports alignment for the first three and one pairwise disagreement with Pass@128.

evidence_standards.name: 128 proof attempts per theorem; Lean 4.13 verification; maximum proof length of 2048 tokens
evidence_standards.detail: These are the stated proof-generation and verification settings for the reported evaluations.

evidence_standards.name: Adaptive-score convergence criterion
evidence_standards.detail: The score is treated as converged when its change is less than 0.01 for 10 consecutive rounds.

datasets.name: FormL4
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated on Random Test (950 items), Basic Test (970), and Real Test (967). Random Test is a random Mathlib 4 theorem split; Basic Test contains foundational theorems from mathematical topics; Real Test is built from natural-language questions and answers from Li et al. (2024), converted into statements by appending the ground-truth answer and a request to prove it. Autoformalization is scored by the percentage of generated outputs that compile with Lean 4; reported table results use greedy decoding.

metrics.name: Compiler success rate (greedy score)
metrics.caveat: Lean 4 compilation checks formal proof correctness but cannot establish semantic correspondence between the formal statement and the natural-language input; the paper also reports human evaluation.

metrics.name: Human evaluation score
metrics.caveat: The compiler alone falls short of evaluating strict semantic alignment; human experts evaluate whether natural-language statements were successfully translated into formal statements.

controls.name: Outcome-Supervised Verifier (OSV)
controls.detail: Verifier trained with a single final compilation outcome as its label, compared with the process-supervised verifier trained using first-error-location step labels.
controls.rules_out: That the verifier improvement is explained by verifier training alone rather than process-level supervision.

controls.name: RFT-only autoformalizer
controls.detail: Rejective-sampling fine-tuning without the verifier-enhancement component, compared with RFT+VEA.
controls.rules_out: That the combined model’s improvement is due only to rejective sampling rather than the added verifier component.

controls.name: Baseline Autoformalizer
controls.detail: The FormL4-finetuned baseline, compared with enhanced autoformalizers.
controls.rules_out: That the reported enhancement is merely the effect of the baseline FormL4 fine-tuning.

confounds.name: Compiler success may reflect formal validity without semantic alignment to the input
confounds.detail: A generated statement and proof can compile even if the formal statement does not mean the same thing as the natural-language statement; the authors identify this as a limitation of compiler-only validation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Human evaluation of autoformalizer outputs for successful translation of natural-language statements into formal statements; the study also compares human scores for baseline and enhanced outputs.

evidence_standards.name: Human evaluation study size and sampling
evidence_standards.detail: Evaluates 60 samples, with 20 each from the Random, Basic, and Real test sets; samples are grouped so half have true proof validity and half false. The paper reports that the enhanced-versus-baseline human-score difference is not statistically significant.

evidence_standards.name: ANOVA significance testing
evidence_standards.detail: Human-evaluation significance tests use ANOVA; table markers specify * for p<0.05, ** for p<0.01, and *** for p<0.001. The paper reports p=0.002992 for Proof Validity and p=0.000002 for Dataset Split.

evidence_standards.name: Greedy decoding
evidence_standards.detail: The FormL4 model comparison table reports compiler-success percentages under greedy decoding.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: A small fully connected 3-layer network was trained on MNIST. The evaluation arbitrarily selected 10 labeled source images from the MNIST test set and tested all 9 other target labels for each image (90 experiments per network and distance metric), using both L1 and L∞ distortion. For the defense comparison, the paper used the 35 L∞ instances on which Reluplex terminated for both networks.

baselines.name: Carlini–Wagner (CW) attack
baselines.fair_comparison: For each network, source image, target label, and distance metric, CW produced the initial targeted adversarial example; its distortion was compared with the Reluplex result for the same instance.

baselines.name: Untrained network N
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared with adversarially trained network N̄ on the same 35 source-target instances where Reluplex terminated for both, using L∞ distance.

metrics.name: Adversarial-example distortion (L1 and L∞)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports average CW and minimally distorted distances. For timed-out Reluplex runs, it uses the last, smallest δmax found; it also reports results on terminated experiments separately from results including all 90.

metrics.name: Percent improvement over CW
metrics.caveat: The reported averages can conceal individual cases where CW is substantially suboptimal; the paper notes gaps of 30–40% in some cases and reports target-specific variation.

metrics.name: Reluplex termination count
metrics.caveat: A termination count below 90 means some distances are not fully resolved; the all-experiment results use the last δmax before timeout.

metrics.name: Network nonlinearity
metrics.caveat: Defined as the number of ReLU units switching between the saturated-zero and linear regions from the source input to the adversarial example; the paper reports no statistically significant difference between networks.

controls.name: Untrained network N
controls.detail: The adversarially trained network N̄ was compared against the original, untrained N on the same 35 L∞ instances for which both Reluplex runs terminated.
controls.rules_out: That the observed robustness increase is merely an artifact of evaluating different source-target instances.

confounds.name: Adversarial training only overfits to the attack used during training
confounds.detail: The apparent improvement might reflect resistance to the training attack rather than increased robustness more generally.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The minimally distorted examples improved over CW by about 12% on both the hardened and untrained networks; the authors report no evidence of overfitting.

confounds.name: The hardened network is easier to verify only because it uses fewer ReLU nonlinearities
confounds.detail: Its higher Reluplex termination rate might be due to reduced nonlinearity rather than another property of the network.
confounds.ruled_out_by: They counted ReLU units switching between saturated and linear regions between each source and adversarial example, and found no statistically significant difference between the networks.

confounds.name: The defense only makes existing attacks fail, without increasing true robustness
confounds.detail: A defense could appear effective against current attacks while leaving the nearest adversarial example just as close.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Reluplex was used to find provably minimally distorted adversarial examples, and the paper compared their distances for the trained and untrained networks.

confounds.name: The selected examples may not represent the networks' broader behavior
confounds.detail: The reported average robustness increase could depend on the arbitrarily selected source points; the paper notes that some individual instances became less robust after training.

evidence_standards.name: Reluplex search precision
evidence_standards.detail: Binary search shrinks δmax−δmin below 10^-3; the returned δmax is stated to be accurate to that precision.

evidence_standards.name: Statistical significance for the nonlinearity comparison
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says there was no statistically significant difference between networks, but does not specify the test, number of runs or seeds, variance reporting, or a significance threshold.

datasets.name: Mizar Mathematical Library (MML), version 4.181.114711
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the 32,524 theorems known to be ATP-provable given suitable premises. Randomly holds out 3,124 statements; uses 400 for monitoring and model/checkpoint selection, and evaluates on the remaining 2,724 conjectures (the results table labels the test set 2,742). Only conjectures are held out; all statements are available as axioms. Premise candidates are chronologically preceding statements. Mizar formulas are translated to first-order logic by MPTP. E prover uses its auto strategy, with 90-second soft and 120-second hard time limits, 4 GB memory, and a 500,000 processed-clause limit; it is run on the top k ranked premises for k=16, 32, …, 1024 until a proof is found or k=1024 fails. The paper also applies two models to previously unproven Mizar statements and reports 823 additional proofs.

baselines.name: Distance-weighted k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) with handcrafted semantic features
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper says k-NN is trained on all statements as axioms, as are the neural models; both rank the chronologically preceding statements as premise candidates for held-out conjectures and are evaluated using the same E prover setup.

metrics.name: Number and percentage of conjectures proved from the top-k premises
metrics.caveat: The paper says this primary metric accommodates alternative proofs but is computationally expensive; it also reports average maximum relative rank (aMRR) as a ranking-quality measure.

metrics.name: Average maximum relative rank (aMRR)
metrics.caveat: It is nonzero even when every true dependency is ranked ahead of false dependencies (the stated best possible value is 0.051). For continuous monitoring, the paper approximates it using all true dependencies and 128 fixed random false dependencies for each of 400 held-out conjectures.

controls.name: Word-CNN with random starting embeddings
controls.detail: An otherwise similar word-embedding model uses random starting embeddings rather than definition embeddings from a character-level model.
controls.rules_out: A comparison with the definition-embedding model tests whether the reported advantage is simply from using a word-level model; the random-start model is reported to overfit after about 250,000 iterations and underperform the best character-level model.

controls.name: Training without hard negative mining
controls.detail: The paper reports results for models trained without hard negative mining alongside those trained with it.
controls.rules_out: Whether the gains associated with hard negative mining require that training mechanism rather than arising from the model training setup alone; the paper reports that mining doubles the number proved at top-16 and improves the union-of-cutoffs proof ratio for the best neural model from 61.3% to 66.4%.

confounds.name: Learning from future proofs because the train/test conjecture split is randomized
confounds.detail: A proof of a theorem written later in the corpus could guide premise selection for an earlier theorem, making results look strong even if the method does not generalize under chronological evaluation.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The authors cite previous k-NN experiments showing similar performance under full 10-fold cross-validation and incremental evaluation, provided chronologically preceding formulas participate in proofs only of later theorems. They do not report this comparison specifically for the neural models.

evidence_standards.name: Random-initialization runs and variance
evidence_standards.detail: For each architecture, the authors trained three models with different random initialization seeds. The plotted results show only the best runs; they report seeing little variance between runs of the same architecture.

evidence_standards.name: E prover evaluation resource limits
evidence_standards.detail: Reported proof results use E prover's auto strategy with a 90-second soft time limit, 120-second hard time limit, 4 GB memory limit, and 500,000 processed-clause limit.
